rows.description: A toddler claps when others clap and waves along with a group song. Joining in shows delight and belonging, and imitation is how children learn shared signals.
A teenager joins a school vigil or memorial, showing grief and solidarity with silence, flowers or lamps. Each participant may feel different things, and some may cry while others feel numb.

A young adult joins hashtags, petitions, group chats or shared black-profile-picture moments to show solidarity. Digital unity is easy to join and quick to fade, and it works best paired with real support.
After the match ends a child says he knew that team would lose. The mind quietly rewrites earlier uncertainty into a neat, predictable story.
A teenager whose friend failed an exam says it was obvious, ignoring that the outcome looked open beforehand. Judging past choices by known results is unfair to the decider.

rows.subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
rows.description: A child begs to try the tallest slide and every new game; excitement and challenge feel like life itself, and boredom feels worse than a little risk.

rows.subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
rows.description: A young adult stands for student leadership to shape decisions and be respected; the wish for influence can serve a group well or slide into wanting control over others.

rows.subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
rows.description: A young professional chooses a steady job and saves carefully, valuing certainty and safety for family over chances; calm and worry can both come with the choice.

A teenager who falls silent or stops abruptly mid-sentence may be hurt, embarrassed, angry or simply thinking. Silence is ambiguous, so a caring reply gives space and leaves the door open to talk later.

In some Indian and other group settings overlapping speech signals engagement, while in others it signals disrespect. A young professional watches the local norm before judging someone as rude or passive.
A child cries harder over losing a marble than he celebrates winning one. Giving up something owned feels heavier than getting an equal thing.

rows.subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager avoids trying a new sport or friend group because losing his current standing feels worse than any possible gain. Safe choices shrink his world.
A young adult holds a losing stock or a failing project too long to avoid the pain of realising the loss, while selling winners too soon.
A toddler explores, checks back with a caregiver, protests at parting and is soothed on return. Trust that comfort will come lets the child venture out, and feelings can be shown openly.
A child makes friends, handles quarrels and asks for help without shame. Assumes people generally mean well, and can recover after a disagreement.
A young adult can say what they need, tolerate a partner's need for space and repair after fights. Closeness and independence coexist without constant fear of loss.
